catalog_citation: Green, Ian. 1989. Marrithiyel: a language of the Daly River region of Australia's Northern Territory. PhD thesis, Australian National University. xiv+410 pp.http://hdl.handle.net/1885/10926(open access).
catalog_locator: Section 2.1.3 'Word Stress', pp. 33-39 (page offset 15); quote from p. 33, p. 34 and the summary rules on p. 39; orthography note 5 (p. 65) for the digraphs /ng/, /nj/ used in the syllable count.
catalog_quote: Apart from reduplications, each phonological word has one primary, and, where possible, one secondary stress. Stress is cued by both pitch and loudness, with stressed syllables being perceptibly higher in pitch and louder than unstressed syllables. [p. 33] ... Primary stress is normally assigned to the first syllable of a stem, and secondary stress to the second syllable thereafter. For unprefixed nominals this results simply in primary stress falling on the initial syllable of the word [p. 34] ... The principles of stress assignment can thus be stated as follows: (1) Primary stress is placed on the first syllable of each reduplicating sequence. (2) Otherwise, primary stress falls, for verbs, on the first syllable of the complex verb stem, and, for nominals, on the first syllable of the nominal stem. (The "stem" for nominals is the minimal independent grammatical unit). (3) In the absence of a syllabic stem (as is the case, for example, with "simple" verbs) primary stress falls on the first syllable of the word. (4) Secondary stress is placed on the second unstressed syllable after each primary stress. (5) If the initial syllable of the word is unstressed, and not adjacent to a primary stressed syllable, it also receives a secondary stress. [p. 39]
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.check: quotation verified in source (minor differences in wording)
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Opened (425 pp., ANU Acrobat paper-capture text; no scanned needed) and re-extracted printed pp. 33-39 = pp. 48-54 with extracted text (page offset 15, consistent with p. 13 = PDF 28). Section 2.1.3 "Word Stress" is there. The p. 34 sentence is verbatim: "Primary stress is normally assigned to the first syllable of a stem, and secondary stress to the second syllable thereafter. For unprefixed nominals this results simply in primary stress falling on the initial syllable of the word, e.g.:". The p. 39 summary rules (1)-(4) are verbatim as quoted, with one silent omission: after rule (2) the source has the parenthetical "(The "stem" for nominals is the minimal independent grammatical unit)."…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Each phonological word has one primary stress (cued by higher pitch and loudness), placed on the first syllable of the stem: for nominals the first syllable of the nominal stem (grammatical class prefixes a-, mi-, ma- are skipped, but lexicalised a-/mi- count as stem), for verbs the first syllable of the complex verb stem that follows the auxiliary (so the pronominal/auxiliary prefixes are unstressed). Reduplicated roots each carry a primary stress, overriding the stem rule. If there is no syllabic stem (simple verbs), primary stress falls on the first syllable of the word. So stress is stem-initial rather than word-initial: word-initial only in unprefixed words.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Secondary stress on the second unstressed syllable after each primary stress (i.e. alternating rightward); additionally the word-initial syllable takes a secondary stress if it is unstressed and not adjacent to a primary-stressed syllable (rule 5, p. 39). Secondary is weaker in both pitch and loudness (pp. 33-34).
new_statements.exceptions: Reduplications have two (or more) primary stresses, one per reduplicant, which take precedence over stem-initial stress (pp. 35-38). Simple verbs with no syllabic stem: word-initial stress (p. 39). Verb root /it/ 'pick up' loses its vowel after a vowel-final auxiliary, and stress then reverts to word-initial (p. 37). Compound language name 'Marri Ammu' pronounced as two phonological words with two primary stresses (p. 13 n.5). The 1981 MA analysis (pp. 26-32) had extra shift rules (e.g. primary stress on the medial syllable of a trisyllabic word in one environment) that the 1989 thesis revised (1989 p. 44 n.1).
new_statements.domain_note: Phonological word (Green explicitly says 'each phonological word'); the description is based on fieldwork elicitation and texts, not instrumental; stress said to be cued by pitch and loudness. In serial transitive+intransitive verb constructions the second verb is a separate phonological word for stress (1989 p. 224).
new_statements.identity_note: Green 1989 describes Marrithiyel proper ('paperbark language', also called Brinken/Berringen), spoken around the Daly River, NT, from fieldwork with Marrithiyel speakers; Green (1989 §1.4, pp. 14-16) treats Marridan, Marri Ammu and Marrisjabin as its dialects, which Glottolog subsumes under mari1424 (Tryon 1974 spells them Maridan, MareAmmu, Marityabin). The stress statement is for Marrithiyel proper. Green 1981 (MA) used a different orthography (ty, k, p) and a slightly different stress analysis, revised in 1989.

tone_statements.citation: Stanner, W. E. H. 1938. Notes on the Marithiel language. Oceania 9(1): 101-108.
tone_statements.quote: The language is pitched fairly high, and in any general conversation a great use is made of tonal variation. Correct stress appears to be of great importance in correct speech. Several words with a common form are only to be distinguished in this way.

sources.note: Section 2.1.3 'Word Stress' pp. 33-39: one primary stress per phonological word, cued by pitch and loudness; primary stress on the first syllable of the stem (nominal stem; complex verb stem in verbs, so verb-initial auxiliary/pronominal prefixes are unstressed); each reduplicant gets a primary stress; secondary stress on the second unstressed syllable after each primary; word-initial syllable gets secondary stress if unstressed and not adjacent to a primary; summary rules (1)-(5) on p. 39.

sources.citation: Green, Ian. 1981. The phonology and morphology of Marrithiyel: a preliminary study. MA thesis, Australian National University. vii+170 pp.http://hdl.handle.net/1885/11089
sources.note: Section 2.3 'Word Stress' pp. 26-32: 'Except in cases of reduplication each Marrithiyel word carries only one primary stress. It is my impression that stress is mainly cued by a rise in pitch. Primary stress is normally placed on the first syllable of the stem. Where possible a secondary stress is placed on the second syllable after the primary stress' (p. 26); prefixes unstressed; six summary rules p. 30. Superseded by Green 1989 (1989 p. 44 n.1: stress assignment revised).

tone.quote: The language is pitched fairly high, and in any general conversation a great use is made of tonal variation. Correct stress appears to be of great importance in correct speech. Several words with a common form are only to be distinguished in this way.
tone.says: Impressionistic: the language 'is pitched fairly high' and conversation makes 'great use of tonal variation' (i.e. intonation); the functional prosodic contrast Stanner reports is STRESS ('Several words with a common form are only to be distinguished in this way'; first syllable of disyllables always stressed). No claim of lexical tone; no tone inventory.
